title: Education Beyond Seat Time Aldeman, Chad
author: Aldeman, Chad
summary: Education policy analyst Chad Aldeman examines the persistent appeal and consistent failure of competency-based education (CBE) as an alternative to the century-old seat-time credit system. While CBE's logic -- advance when you've mastered the material rather than when the clock runs out -- is sound in theory, its implementation consistently degrades into a fast-pass mechanism rather than a more rigorous path to genuine mastery. Aldeman engages directly with the behavioral economics of how students actually allocate effort: without external time structure, most defer, delay, and scramble, producing last-minute cramming with a competency label stamped on it. He argues a well-designed CBE system would need to continuously re-engage students through retrieval, application, and spiraling revisitation -- essentially rebuilding the external structure CBE was designed to eliminate.
points: Competency-based education has been 'the most promising alternative' to seat-time for decades yet remains confined to credit recovery and alternative programs -- a pattern suggesting systemic implementation challenges rather than isolated execution failures.

The theoretical advantage of CBE inverts in practice because students under flexible timelines behave as if they have unlimited time, producing procrastination, end-loaded effort, and surface mastery that doesn't survive retention intervals.

Genuine mastery requires not just initial achievement but durable retention across time and varied application contexts -- a standard CBE programs rarely specify, defaulting instead to one-time demonstration of proficiency.

A defensible CBE system would need retrieval practice across multiple sessions, spaced revisitation, and transfer tasks -- requirements that effectively rebuild the temporal structure CBE was designed to escape.

The credit-hour system's persistence is not merely institutional inertia; it encodes genuine functions -- preventing procrastination, forcing regular engagement -- that CBE designers must replace, not simply remove.
quotes: For over a century, American education has mostly organized itself around time. Students earn credits by sitting through a prescribed number of hours of instruction regardless of what they actually learn. This system was designed for administrative purposes, not as a way to measure learning.
